title: Christopher Gist, 1750–51
summary: In 1750 the Ohio Company of Virginia sent surveyor Christopher Gist west on a journey that produced one of the earliest English accounts of Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
In the autumn of 1750 the Ohio Company of Virginia sent the surveyor Christopher Gist west to look at the lands it hoped to claim. The [National Park Service's profile of Christopher Gist](https://www.nps.gov/people/christopher-gist.htm) says the company hired him for £150 to explore the Ohio country as far as the Falls of the Ohio. His journey of 1750–51 produced one of the earliest English written accounts of the country that became Kentucky.

## Into the Ohio country

The [Ohio Company](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ohio_Company) was a group of Virginia land speculators seeking a royal grant west of the mountains. Gist's job was to find good land and to meet the Native nations who already lived and traded there.

According to [a biography of Gist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Gist), he spent Christmas Day 1750 at Muskingum, where he held a Church of England service with local Native people. In January 1751 he reached [Lower Shawneetown](/stories/lower-shawneetown-at-the-scioto-mouth/), at the mouth of the Scioto River, traveling with the trader George Croghan, the interpreter Andrew Montour and Robert Callender. [Lower Shawnee Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Shawnee_Town) records that the party met in council with the Shawnee leader Big Hannaona. Gist stayed about 12 days and described a wedding festival in the town.

In February 1751 he was well received at Pickawillany on the Great Miami River. There he strengthened the alliance between the Miami leader Memeskia and British interests against the French. These visits show that the Ohio Valley was a crowded, political place. Shawnee, Wyandot, Miami and other nations were weighing British and French offers on their own terms.

## Crossing into Kentucky

From the Shawnee country, Gist crossed the Ohio into what is now Kentucky. [Grokipedia's article on Gist](https://grokipedia.com/page/Christopher_Gist) dates the crossing to around March 3, 1751, and says his journal described buffalo, canebrakes and rich land. He traveled with a Black servant, whose name the sources checked do not give. The NPS says Gist explored areas previously unseen by English colonists, such as Kentucky.

Gist did not reach the Falls. From Kentucky he returned to his home on the Yadkin River in North Carolina. Some accounts say he visited [Big Bone Lick](/stories/big-bone-lick-older-cycle/) in March 1751. That claim is disputed, and this story does not rely on it.

## What the journey led to

Gist's report fed the Ohio Company's plans and Virginia's diplomacy. Grokipedia says that at the 1752 [Treaty of Logstown](/stories/treaty-of-logstown-1752/) he presented the company's charter to Iroquois, Shawnee and Delaware delegates. Competition between Britain and France for the Ohio Valley soon turned into the French and Indian War.

Gist was not the only early English visitor. In the spring of 1750, Dr. Thomas Walker had led a Loyal Land Company party through [Cumberland Gap](/stories/thomas-walker-and-cumberland-gap/) into southeastern Kentucky. The two journeys together mark the start of written English descriptions of Kentucky. For the Shawnee, Cherokee and other nations, the land had long been home, hunting ground and trade route.

## Kentucky today

No single marker traces Gist's route across Kentucky, and his exact path is still debated. His journal remains a primary source for historians of the Ohio Valley in 1751. The Falls of the Ohio, the goal he never reached, has [its own story](/stories/falls-of-the-ohio/) in this collection.
